entities.name: A Thousand Splendid Suns
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
A Thousand Splendid Suns, published in 2007, is a seminal work by Afghan-American author Khaled Hosseini that captures the tumultuous history and struggles of women in Afghanistan over the last four decades of social and political upheaval. Set against the backdrop of the Soviet invasion, the rise of the Taliban, and subsequent conflicts, the narrative intertwines the lives of two women, Mariam and Laila, symbolizing resilience amidst oppression. Hosseini's portrayal of their bond, set in cities like Herat and Kabul, highlights the systemic gender-based violence and societal constraints faced by Afghan women, rendering it a crucial text in contemporary discussions on gender and human rights in the region.

The novel's narrative arc spans from the 1960s, showcasing the drastic transitions in Afghan society as the nation shifts from relative stability to war and chaos. Mariam, born out of wedlock, endures a life of shame and hardship, while Laila enjoys a more privileged upbringing until a tragic event forces her to marry Mariam's abusive husband, Rasheed. This intersecting of lives illustrates the collapsing familial structures and the harsh realities imposed by patriarchal norms. Through their struggles and ultimate solidarity, Hosseini critiques the broader sociopolitical conditions that have historically marginalized women in Afghanistan, making the novel a poignant commentary on the intersection of personal and political narratives.
